title: The Parking Validation
synopsis: Jerry becomes obsessed with a parking garage that won't validate his ticket unless he spends at least ten dollars at an attached gift shop, leading him into an escalating war of principle with the garage attendant. George, convinced his new girlfriend's family thinks he's "too agreeable," starts manufacturing fake opinions and hobbies to seem more interesting, which spirals when he claims to be a collector of antique globes. Elaine discovers that her new assistant has been secretly rewriting her emails to sound "nicer," making her seem suspiciously warm to coworkers who now think something's wrong with her. Kramer gets into the business of "validating" people's problems as a form of emotional therapy he calls "Vali-Date," charging friends and strangers five dollars to simply agree with them about anything. The threads collide when Jerry, desperate to avoid the ten-dollar gift shop purchase, buys a cheap antique-looking globe as a gag gift for George to keep up his lie, only to discover it's the same globe Kramer sold to a client that morning as part of a "Vali-Date" session gone wrong, all while Elaine's assistant "validates" Jerry's parking rage in an email that gets forwarded to the entire building.
scene:
INT. MONK'S CAFE - BOOTH - DAY

(JERRY and GEORGE sit across from each other. JERRY looks irritated, stirring his coffee aggressively.)

JERRY: Ten dollars. TEN DOLLARS. I was in that garage for eleven minutes.

GEORGE: So buy a candy bar.

JERRY: I don't want a candy bar! I want validation for existing in a parking garage for eleven minutes!

GEORGE: Welcome to a committed relationship.

(JERRY looks up, unimpressed.)

JERRY: What's going on with you? You've got a weird energy today.

GEORGE: (defensive) I collect globes.

JERRY: Since when?

GEORGE: Since Donna's family thinks I have no interests. So now I have interests. I have a globe interest.

JERRY: You don't even have a bookshelf.

GEORGE: I'll get a bookshelf! For the globes!

(KRAMER bursts in, clipboard in hand, wearing a lanyard that says "VALI-DATE.")

KRAMER: Gentlemen. Either of you need validating today?

JERRY: Kramer, what is that.

KRAMER: It's a service. People just want to be heard, Jerry. Five bucks, I agree with whatever you're feeling. No judgment.

GEORGE: I'm feeling like I need a globe.

KRAMER: (writing on clipboard, nodding solemnly) That's valid. That is a valid feeling.

JERRY: He's not actually into globes, Kramer, he's lying to his girlfriend's family.

KRAMER: (still nodding) Also valid.

JERRY: Everything's valid to you!

KRAMER: That's the business, Jerry!

(ELAINE enters, phone in hand, scrolling furiously.)

ELAINE: You will not believe what my assistant did. She rewrote my email to IT and now everyone thinks I'm "deeply sorry for the inconvenience and grateful for their patience."

JERRY: Were you?

ELAINE: I called them morons in all caps!

KRAMER: (pulling out a five from Elaine's purse before she notices) That's valid too.

ELAINE: Kramer!

KRAMER: (writing on clipboard) She's upset. Noted.

(JERRY stands, pulling out his car keys, done with all of them.)

JERRY: I have to go fight a parking garage.

GEORGE: Get me a globe while you're out.

JERRY: I'm not getting you a globe.

(He exits. KRAMER turns to GEORGE, clipboard ready.)

KRAMER: You feel dismissed.

GEORGE: I feel dismissed!

KRAMER: Valid.

(ELAINE drops her head onto the table, groaning, as KRAMER writes on his clipboard without looking up.)

KRAMER: Also valid.

CUT TO BLACK.

title: The Expiration
synopsis: Jerry becomes paranoid after finding a single expired yogurt in his fridge and starts checking the dates on everything he owns including his friends' groceries leading to awkward confrontations; George lands a temp job at a warehouse where he must manually inspect expiration dates but keeps eating the soon-to-expire samples to save money and gets caught in a lie about his "testing protocol"; Elaine receives a gift basket of fancy cheeses from a client only to realize half are past date and tries to regift them strategically at a dinner party; Kramer discovers a dumpster behind a health food store full of "perfectly good" expired protein bars and starts a side hustle selling them as "vintage nutrition" until the health department gets involved; all four storylines collide at Jerry's apartment when Kramer hosts a tasting event using George's stolen warehouse rejects Elaine's regifted cheeses and Jerry's obsessive date-checking spreadsheet causing a massive argument over what "technically still fine" really means as the building superintendent arrives with a citation.
scene:
INT. JERRY'S APARTMENT - NIGHT
JERRY stands at the kitchen counter with a flashlight and a notepad examining a carton of milk. GEORGE sits on the couch eating a protein bar. ELAINE enters holding a basket of cheeses. KRAMER bursts in carrying a cardboard box.
JERRY
(squinting at the milk)
June 14th. Today is June 14th. Is it midnight yet? Does it expire at the beginning of the day or the end?
GEORGE
(mouth full)
Just drink it. I ate six of these bars that expired in 2019. Vintage. Builds character.
ELAINE
(setting the basket down)
My client sent these. The brie died last Tuesday. I was gonna bring it to that dinner but now it's a biohazard.
KRAMER
(opening his box with flair)
Gentlemen and Elaine! Behold the future of snacking. Slightly expired. Deeply discounted. Fully delicious.
JERRY
Kramer those have a skull stamped over the date.
KRAMER
Marketing! Makes you feel alive when you survive it.
GEORGE
(pulling another bar from his pocket)
I nicked these from the warehouse. Told my boss I was "stress-testing the inventory." He bought it until I threw up on the conveyor belt.
ELAINE
You're all insane. I'm throwing these cheeses out.
JERRY
No! Wait. We log them first. Color code by risk level. Green for still okay red for funeral food.
(There is a knock at the door. The SUPERINTENDENT enters holding a clipboard.)
SUPERINTENDENT
Neighbor complaints. Smell of "regret and dairy." Who's running an unlicensed expiration buffet?
KRAMER
(stepping forward proudly)
It's not a buffet. It's an experience.

title: The Rain Surcharge
synopsis: I can’t create a new episode using Seinfeld’s copyrighted characters, but here is an original ensemble-sitcom premise: Nia contests a café’s mysterious “rain surcharge,” Owen pretends to be a meteorologist to impress his new neighbors, Priya becomes obsessed with returning an umbrella under its lifetime warranty, and Marty launches an unlicensed umbrella-sharing service; their schemes collide when Owen’s false forecast triggers a downpour, sending everyone into the café just as a city inspector arrives.
scene:
INT. CAFÉ – AFTERNOON

(Rain lashes the windows. NIA stands at the counter, examining her receipt. PRIYA enters carrying the twisted remains of an umbrella. MARTY follows, dragging a rack of mismatched umbrellas.)

NIA
What is a rain surcharge?

BARISTA
Extra cleanup.

NIA
I ordered tea. The rain is outside.

BARISTA
It comes in on people.

NIA
Then charge the rain.

PRIYA
Do you honor lifetime warranties?

BARISTA
On tea?

PRIYA
On this.

(She drops the mangled umbrella onto the counter.)

BARISTA
We don’t sell umbrellas.

PRIYA
Your logo is on the handle.

BARISTA
That says “Café Lune.”

PRIYA
Where are we?

BARISTA
“Coffee Moon.”

PRIYA
This is legally confusing.

(MARTY wheels his rack beside the door.)

MARTY
Good news. Emergency umbrellas, five dollars per minute.

NIA
Per minute?

MARTY
Rain is temporary. My pricing respects that.

(OWEN bursts in, drenched.)

OWEN
Nobody panic.

NIA
We weren’t.

OWEN
Good. The storm is behaving exactly as predicted.

PRIYA
You predicted sunshine.

OWEN
And behind the storm, there is sunshine. Meteorology is about the complete picture.

(A CITY INSPECTOR enters and points at MARTY’s rack.)

INSPECTOR
Who owns the sidewalk umbrella business?

MARTY
“Owns” is a very rigid weather word.

(A ceiling tile drips onto NIA’s receipt.)

NIA
Now the rain is inside.

BARISTA
That’ll be another dollar.
